A judge ordered Thursday for President Donald Trump to sit for a deposition as part of his $10 billion defamation lawsuit against the British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC).
U.S. Magistrate Judge Enjoliqué Lett said Trump must give his deposition by Dec. 11 unless the discovery deadline is extended beyond Dec. 18.
This followed complaints by the BBC’s legal counsel about the delay in the deposition after Trump had canceled a previously scheduled deposition for Oct.16.
TRUMP THREATENED BY JUDGE WITH SANCTIONS IF HE DOESN’T SIT FOR DEPOSITION IN $10 BILLION BBC DEFAMATION SUIT
“The formerly respected and now disgraced BBC defamed President Trump by intentionally, maliciously, and deceptively doctoring his speech in a brazen attempt to interfere in the 2024 Presidential Election,” a spokesperson for Trump’s legal team told Fox News Digital. “The BBC has a long pattern of deceiving its audience in coverage of President Trump, all in service of its own leftist political agenda. President Trump’s powerhouse lawsuit is holding the BBC accountable for its defamation and reckless election interference just as he has held other fake news mainstream media responsible for their wrongdoing.”
A spokesperson for the BBC declined to comment.
JUDGE LIMITS BBC FROM RELITIGATING JAN 6 IN TRUMP LAWSUIT OVER MISLEADING DOCUMENTARY EDIT
The BBC previously filed a motion to compel Trump’s deposition. The BBC had said it understood that Trump’s deposition requires “additional planning,” and he “accepted the obligations of civil litigation” when he chose to file the lawsuit.
Trump filed a $10 billion lawsuit against the BBC late last year for its 2024 “Panorama” documentary that distorted his remarks to supporters on Jan. 6, 2021. Critics claim the documentary was misleading because it omitted Trump’s call for supporters to protest peacefully, splicing together separate portions of a lengthy address to give a wrong impression.
“We’re going to walk down to the Capitol. And I’ll be there with you. And we fight — we fight like hell,” the documentary showed Trump saying.
In reality, Trump said, “We’re going to walk down to the Capitol. And we’re going to cheer on our brave senators and congressmen and women, and we’re probably not going to be cheering so much for some of them, because you’ll never take back our country with weakness. You have to show strength, and you have to be strong.”
TRUMP WINS PERMISSION TO FILE AMENDED COMPLAINT IN $10B DEFAMATION LAWSUIT AGAINST BBC
It wasn’t until 54 minutes later that Trump called on his supporters to “fight like hell” for election integrity.
The BBC previously issued an apology for the erroneous edit and said it had pulled the program from its platforms. Despite the apology, the broadcaster has insisted the mistake is not enough for a defamation claim.
The controversy led to the resignations of BBC News CEO Deborah Turness and BBC director-general Tim Davie.

sources.text:
Trump ordered to sit for deposition in BBC defamation lawsuit
Judge says Trump must sit for questioning from a BBC lawyer by December 11 or face possible dismissal of lawsuit.
A federal judge in the United States has ordered President Donald Trump to sit for a deposition as part of his $10bn defamation lawsuit against the British broadcaster BBC.
On Thursday, US Magistrate Judge Enjolique Lett ruled that Trump would be required to answer questions under oath in a session with the BBC‘s lawyers.
The deposition is scheduled to take place no later than December 11, or Trump could face sanctions, including the possible dismissal of the lawsuit.
Trump had previously been scheduled to sit for deposition on October 16 but had cancelled due to a “matter of national importance”.
Charles Tobin, a lawyer for the BBC, said that the president was in fact campaigning in the state of Georgia on that day.
“He was participating in party politics and prioritised that over sitting for the deposition,” Tobin said.
The BBC lawsuit is one of several he has launched against news outlets over coverage he dislikes or casts as unfair.
Trump is currently enmeshed in another $10bn defamation lawsuit against The Wall Street Journal that he refiled in May after it was previously dismissed. Another defamation case seeks $15bn in damages from The New York Times and Penguin Random House, a book publisher.
That streak of litigation has alarmed press freedom advocates who say that the president frequently uses government pressure and legal threats to shape coverage in his favour.
His case against the BBC centres on a documentary it aired, titled Trump: A Second Chance.
The documentary features clips of a speech Trump made on January 6, 2021, the day that Trump supporters later attacked the US Capitol.
Trump has said that a clip from his speech was misleadingly edited to suggest he encouraged attendees to storm the Capitol, the seat of the US Congress. Legislators inside had been in the process of certifying Trump’s 2020 election defeat at the time of the riot.
The British broadcaster has acknowledged that filmmakers spliced together different segments of Trump’s remarks on January 6.
The head of the BBC and its top news executive both resigned, and the outlet issued an apology. But the network has denied Trump’s defamation claims.
Trump has maintained that he never told his supporters to commit violence in a bid to prevent the peaceful transition of power.
Trump, however, has long pushed the false claim that his loss in the 2020 race was due to election-rigging.
On January 6, 2021, Trump had gathered his supporters on the Ellipse outside the White House to reiterate his unsubstantiated assertions.
During his speech, he encouraged them to “fight like hell” and refused to concede to what he falsely portrayed as an election stolen through “fraud”.
Trump and his allies oversaw a multifaceted effort to stay in power despite his loss, one that included the alleged recruitment of “false electors” to cast fraudulent Electoral College votes on his behalf.
He later faced federal charges of attempting to overturn the 2020 election, which were dropped upon his re-election in 2024.
Separately, a state-level case in Georgia accused Trump of engaging in a criminal conspiracy to subvert the 2020 election. The case was dismissed in November 2025 after a replacement prosecutor took over following the disqualification of Fani Willis, who brought the charges against Trump.
A congressional probe into the events around January 6 concluded that the president had been reluctant to call on his supporters to stand down after they stormed the Capitol.

Oct 22 (Reuters) – A federal judge on Thursday ordered Donald Trump to sit for a deposition by December 11 in his $10 billion defamation lawsuit against the BBC, which has accused the US president of stalling to avoid answering questions under oath, the Associated Press reported.
Trump is suing Britain’s publicly funded broadcaster for at least $10 billion over a misleadingly edited clip of a speech. The case is one of several Trump has privately filed against the news media as part of wider pressure campaign against coverage he dislikes.
US Magistrate Judge Enjolique Lett ordered Trump to take questions from the BBC’s lawyers under oath in a ruling from the bench at a court hearing on Thursday, according to the AP. Trump canceled a deposition in October, citing conflicts with his presidential duties.
Representatives for Trump’s legal team and the BBC did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Trump’s lawsuit filed in December in Florida federal court accuses the BBC of intentionally misleading viewers into thinking he directed supporters to storm the US Capitol by splicing together different parts of a January 6, 2021 speech.
The BBC admitted the edits were misleading and apologized to Trump, though it denies being liable for defamation.
In court filings, the broadcaster has accused Trump and his lawyers of dragging their feet in response to their requests for records and other information that is exchanged between parties in a process known as discovery.
The BBC is seeking financial records from Trump’s Mar-a-Lago club and the web of business entities associated with him, saying the information is necessary to defend against Trump’s damages claims.
Trump’s lawyers say the requests are too broad and irrelevant to the case. They have also denied in court filings that Trump is avoiding a deposition, saying Trump’s duties and security needs must take precedence.
The edited speech appeared in a BBC “Panorama” documentary show shortly before the 2024 presidential election, which Trump won. A leaked internal BBC memo cited the edits as evidence of potential political bias, sparking a public relations crisis for the broadcaster and leading to high-level resignations.
(Reporting by Ryan Patrick Jones in Toronto and Jack Queen in New York; editing by Michelle Nichols and Bill Berkrot)

Judge orders Trump to sit for deposition in defamation lawsuit against BBC by Dec. 11
Published 3:35 pm Thursday, October 22, 2026
|                            Getting your Trinity Audio player ready...                        | 
A federal judge on Thursday ordered President Donald Trump to sit for a deposition in his $10 billion defamation lawsuit against the BBC by Dec. 11.
The order from U.S. Magistrate Judge Enjoliqué Lett came as lawyers for the British broadcaster complained that Trump had delayed his appearance. Charles Tobin, attorney for the BBC, said that with two months left in the discovery period, “we still haven’t been able to depose the plaintiff.”
He noted there was an agreed-upon date of Oct. 16, but said Trump had canceled it for a “matter of national importance.” Tobin said the Republican president was in fact campaigning in Georgia that day. “He was participating in party politics and prioritized that over sitting for the deposition,” Tobin said.
Lett said Trump must sit for a deposition by Dec. 11, or face sanctions up to dismissal of his lawsuit -– unless the discovery period is extended past Dec. 18.
Discovery, where lawyers for both sides exchange documents and other evidence, is scheduled to end Dec. 18, and the BBC’s attorneys want to make sure they have Trump’s deposition before that deadline. Lett said only the presiding judge assigned to the case can alter the trial schedule, and the defense said it would be open to scheduling the deposition at a later time if the trial schedule was also moved back.
Trump, who has often avoided depositions, filed his lawsuit against the BBC last December. He accused the publicly funded broadcaster of defamation as well as deceptive and unfair trade practices related to a documentary, “Trump: A Second Chance.”
The BBC acknowledged that filmmakers spliced together quotes from different sections of the speech Trump delivered to his supporters on Jan. 6, 2021, before the storming of the U.S. Capitol, to make it seem he was directly urging violence. The broadcaster apologized over the editing, and the head of the BBC and its top news executive both resigned. But the BBC has denied Trump’s claims that it defamed him.
Trump’s attorneys also argued against recording his deposition on video, asking for only a court reporter. The judge ruled that the deposition could be recorded on video but only for attorneys, meaning it wouldn’t be released to the public.
It remained unclear whether Jack Smith would be allowed to sit for deposition
To bolster its defense, the broadcaster subpoenaed former special counsel Jack Smith earlier this month. Trump’s lawyers have argued that there was no good reason for Smith, who is not a party to the case, to appear.
After arguments Thursday, it was not clear whether Smith would be allowed to sit for a deposition. One issue raised was whether Smith had received the legally required permission from the Department of Justice. Assistant U.S. Attorney Matthew Feeley told the judge that Smith had sent a letter to the department saying he would not testify without permission, and the agency had not yet responded. Lett ordered the department to respond to Smith by Nov. 2.
Earlier in the hearing, Tobin, the BBC lawyer, told the judge that Smith has not objected to being deposed for this case, meaning the only objection is coming from Trump. Tobin said the BBC is not trying to relitigate the events of Jan. 6, but Smith is one of the leading experts in what happened that day, and his deposition could lead the BBC to evidence that could help their case.
“We can argue later on whether his testimony is admissible,” Tobin said, “but we are entitled to that deposition.”
Trump’s lawyer, Alejandro Brito, said Smith has no personal knowledge of Trump’s Jan. 6 speech or Trump’s state of mind when he gave it. All of Smith’s knowledge about the case is secondhand, Brito argued, and the special counsel’s report, along with Smith’s testimony before Congress, is all public and available to the BBC’s attorneys, he said.

sources.news_title: Trump’s $10 Billion BBC Lawsuit Turns Into a Nightmare as Judge Orders Him to Testify — or Face Consequences
sources.text:
Donald Trump’s $10 billion defamation lawsuit against the BBC is turning into a headache after a federal judge ordered the president to sit for a deposition he had desperately tried to avoid, warning that failure to comply could bring sanctions and even get the entire case thrown out.
The order comes after Trump canceled a previously scheduled deposition on October 16, citing a “matter of national importance.” But the BBC’s attorney challenged that explanation, arguing that Trump had instead attended a political rally and fundraiser.
“He was participating in party politics and prioritized that over sitting for the deposition,” Tobin said.
That argument appears to have landed. With the discovery deadline set for December 18, the BBC argued that waiting until late January would leave too little time to complete the evidence-gathering process.
Now, the court has made clear that the deposition cannot simply be put off indefinitely.
U.S. Magistrate Judge Enjoliqué Lett ordered Trump to give a deposition by December 11 or face possible sanctions, including dismissal of his massive defamation lawsuit against the British broadcaster.
And there’s another problem for Trump: he is the person demanding billions of dollars in damages, making his own testimony central to the case.
Trump’s lawyers had argued that the deposition should be postponed. Judge Lett rejected the proposed late-January date, setting December 11 as the deadline.
Now, Trump will have to answer questions under oath on camera unless the court schedule changes or another legal development intervenes.
Trump sued the BBC over a documentary that edited together portions of his January 6, 2021, speech at the Ellipse, before the Capitol attack. He alleges the editing created a false and defamatory impression of his remarks and is seeking $10 billion in damages.
The BBC has acknowledged splicing portions of the speech together but denies that the documentary defamed Trump or caused him damages. The broadcaster has also said the program never aired in the United States.
The BBC has also subpoenaed Trump’s Mar-a-Lago club for information about whether membership applications or fees were affected by the documentary. Trump’s lawyer argued that the request should be thrown out because Trump is not claiming the program harmed the club’s business.
The BBC countered that Trump’s lawsuit alleges damage to his “profession, occupation and trade.” Judge Lett agreed that the information sought falls within the scope of relevant evidence that should be turned over.
That creates another uncomfortable issue for Trump: if he claims the BBC’s documentary damaged his professional standing and cost him billions, the broadcaster argues it should be allowed to investigate evidence relevant to those alleged losses.
Trump has frequently fought efforts to question him in legal disputes, but this case presents a straightforward problem: he voluntarily filed the lawsuit, and the defendant is entitled to seek evidence to challenge his claims.
Trump wants the BBC to pay $10 billion. Now he must sit for a deposition on the court’s schedule—or risk jeopardizing the lawsuit he brought.
The president may be accustomed to setting his own timetable. In this courtroom, however, the judge gets to set the rules.

sources.news_title: Trump Ordered to Testify in UK TV Lawsuit
sources.text:
A US federal judge has ordered Donald Trump to give sworn testimony in his US$10 billion defamation lawsuit against the BBC by 11 December 2026.
A US federal judge in Miami has ordered President Donald Trump to answer questions under oath in his lawsuit against the BBC. The order was issued on Thursday 22 October 2026 and sets a deadline of Friday 11 December 2026.
A sitting US president must now testify in a case he started himself. The ruling was widely reported on Thursday, including by the Puerto Rican outlets El Nuevo Día, El Vocero and Metro Puerto Rico.
Key Facts
—Order. Magistrate Judge Enjoliqué Lett ordered Trump to testify under oath in his BBC lawsuit.
—Deadline. Trump must be deposed by 11 December 2026; evidence-gathering closes on 18 December 2026.
—Claim. Trump seeks US$10 billion over a BBC documentary edit of his 6 January 2021 speech.
—Trial. A two-week trial is provisionally set for 15 February 2027 in Miami.
—As of 22 October 2026, 20:30 GMT
What We Know
In plain English, Trump says a TV edit made it seem he called for a walk to the Capitol. The BBC says it did not defame him, and the judge wants Trump’s sworn answers before the trial.
The order came from US Magistrate Judge Enjoliqué Lett in the Southern District of Florida, which sits in Miami. A magistrate judge is a federal judge who handles pre-trial tasks for the judge who will preside at the trial, here Roy K. Altman.
Trump must give a deposition by 11 December 2026. A deposition is testimony under oath, given outside the courtroom and recorded for use in the case.
The timing matters because discovery closes on Friday 18 December 2026. Discovery is the phase in which each side gathers evidence from the other.
If Trump does not comply, he could face sanctions, including dismissal of his case. That risk would ease only if the court extends discovery beyond 18 December.
Trump had agreed to be deposed on Friday 16 October 2026 and then cancelled. He cited “matters of national importance”, while the BBC’s lawyers say he was campaigning in Georgia that day.
Judge Altman earlier rejected a BBC request to delay discovery, calling it “premature”. A two-week trial is provisionally set for Monday 15 February 2027.
Trump sued in December 2025 for US$10 billion in total. He seeks US$5 billion for defamation and US$5 billion under Florida’s law on deceptive and unfair trade practices.
The suit targets a BBC Panorama documentary, “Trump: A Second Chance?”, broadcast days before the 5 November 2024 US election. It joined parts of Trump’s 6 January 2021 speech that were delivered about 50 minutes apart.
The edit made it appear that he said he would walk to the Capitol with supporters and “fight like hell”. The BBC apologised for the edit, and its director general, Tim Davie, and its head of news resigned over the affair.
The BBC rejects the defamation claim and says it will defend the case. The BBC’s lawyer in the case is Charles Tobin.
What Is Not Known
It is not known whether Trump will sit for the deposition by 11 December 2026. It is also unclear whether the court will extend discovery beyond 18 December.
It is not known whether the BBC will ask the court to dismiss the case. The outcome is unknown, and the trial date of 15 February 2027 is only provisional.
What the Case Means for US Readers
The case tests how far a public figure can hold a broadcaster responsible for an edited programme. Newsrooms everywhere cut and join recorded speeches, so the court’s handling of this edit will be watched by many of them.
The plaintiff is a sitting US president, who must follow the same evidence rules as any other party. The order shows that a president who sues in a US court can be asked to answer questions under oath.
The BBC has apologised for the edit but rejects that it defamed Trump. Those are separate questions, and the court will decide the legal one on the evidence.
Press freedom and the right to seek damages both sit at the centre of this dispute. No court has yet ruled on the claim.
Three dates matter for US readers. They are 11 December 2026 for the deposition, 18 December 2026 for the end of discovery and 15 February 2027 for the provisional trial.
Frequently Asked Questions
What is a deposition?
A deposition is testimony given under oath outside the courtroom. Lawyers from both sides ask questions, and the answers are recorded so they can be used in the case.
When must Trump testify?
Magistrate Judge Enjoliqué Lett ordered him to be deposed by 11 December 2026. Discovery closes on 18 December 2026, and non-compliance could bring sanctions, including dismissal, unless discovery is extended.
Why is Trump suing the BBC?
He says a BBC Panorama documentary, broadcast days before the 5 November 2024 election, edited his 6 January 2021 speech unfairly. He seeks US$10 billion, and the BBC rejects the defamation claim.
When is the trial?
A two-week trial is provisionally set for 15 February 2027 in federal court in Miami. The date could change, and the outcome is unknown.

A US judge has ordered US President Donald Trump to sit for a deposition in his $US10 billion ($14.2 billion) defamation lawsuit against the BBC by December 11.
The order from federal magistrate Judge Enjoliqué Lett on Thursday (US time) came as lawyers for the British broadcaster complained that Trump had delayed his appearance.

He noted there was an agreed-upon date of October 16, but that Trump had cancelled it for a “matter of national importance”. Tobin said the Republican president was in fact campaigning in Georgia that day.
“He was participating in party politics and prioritised that over sitting for the deposition,” Tobin said.
Lett said Trump must sit for a deposition by December 11, or face sanctions up to dismissal of his lawsuit – unless the discovery period was extended past December 18.
Discovery, where lawyers for both sides exchange documents and other evidence, is scheduled to end December 18, and the BBC’s lawyers want to make sure they have Trump’s deposition before that deadline. Lett said only the presiding judge assigned to the case can alter the trial schedule, and the defence said it would be open to scheduling the deposition at a later time if the trial schedule was also moved back.
Trump, who has often avoided depositions, filed his lawsuit against the BBC last December. He accused the publicly funded broadcaster of defamation as well as deceptive and unfair trade practices related to a documentary, Trump: A Second Chance.
The BBC acknowledged that filmmakers spliced together quotes from different sections of the speech Trump delivered to his supporters on January 6, 2021, before the storming of the US Capitol, to make it seem he was directly urging violence. The broadcaster apologised over the editing, and the head of the BBC and its top news executive both resigned. But the BBC has denied Trump’s claims that it defamed him.
To bolster its defence, the broadcaster subpoenaed former special counsel Jack Smith earlier this month. Trump’s lawyers argued, in a joint filing asking for a hearing on the matter, that there was no good reason for Smith, who is not a party to the case, to appear.
The parties were expected to address the issue later in Thursday’s hearing.
“Smith lacks any personal knowledge regarding the issues in this matter,” they argued in the filing. “He was not present when President Trump’s January 6, 2021, speech … was made, nor did he participate in its preparation. Smith does not have any personal knowledge regarding President Trump’s state of mind at the time the speech was given.”
Trump’s side also argued that “Smith’s testimony would be duplicative” because he published a lengthy report on the events of January 6 and also testified for many hours. “The entirety of his testimony is publicly available,” it argued.
The BBC countered, in the same filing, that there were few more knowledgeable sources about the events of January 6 than Smith, who studied and investigated them for years.
“It is difficult to imagine a more authoritative source on these issues than Mr Smith, who spent years gathering evidence on those topics with the force of the Justice Department and the power of the grand jury behind him,” the BBC’s lawyers argued.
“No one forced [the] plaintiff to file this lawsuit and to dispute that his speech on January 6 incited the violence that followed at the Capitol. sources.news_title: Judge insists Trump must be deposed in his $10B lawsuit against the BBC, warns it could be tossed in fight over records
sources.text:
Judge insists Trump must be deposed in his $10B lawsuit against the BBC, warns it could be tossed in fight over records
By Tierney Sneed, CNN
Miami (CNN) — A federal judge warned President Donald Trump could see his $10 billion defamation lawsuit against the BBC dismissed if he does not work harder to produce information the news outlet is entitled to in the case, including sitting for a deposition.
“Engaging in discovery is burdensome, but is a burden we undertake, especially if we file a lawsuit,” Magistrate Judge Enjoliqué Aytch Lett told personal attorneys for Trump at a hearing Thursday, where she also backed a subpoena from the BBC for membership records at Mar-a-Lago.
Lett expressed skepticism that Trump and his team had done an adequate job searching for internal documents related to the case.
“I tend to agree with the defendant that it strains credulity that a thorough search has been in order to determine that all of the requests have been responded to,” she said.
Lett also ordered that Trump sit for a deposition by December 11, but she and both parties said there was a likely possibility it could be moved back. She also rejected Trump’s request to prevent his deposition from being videotaped, but said that only attorneys in the case could see it.
The proceedings showed how the president’s litigiousness comes with risks, including that lawsuits can expose Trump and his businesses to scrutiny from the parties he is suing.
Trump filed the lawsuit against the BBC in December 2025. He alleges he was defamed by the media company with a documentary on his political comeback that aired before the 2024 election, because of how the film spliced two parts of the January 6, 2021, speech he gave in front of the White House before his supporters violently attacked the US Capitol.
The documentary joined one section of his remarks, in which he told his supporters to “walk down to the Capitol,” with a later portion, in which he told the protestors that “we fight like hell.”
The dispute over the president’s deposition was before the judge after Trump’s lawyers abruptly cancelled plans for him to sit for questioning last Friday, citing matters of “national importance.” BBC’s attorneys, however, noted that Trump spent that day on the campaign trail in Georgia and fundraising from Mar-a-Lago, with the company’s lawyer, Chuck Tobin, arguing Thursday that the president had “prioritized party politics” over his obligations to the court.
Trump attorney Alejandro Brito pushed back on that characterization, telling the judge, “It insults the intelligence of everyone in this courtroom” to suggest those two events were the only things the president was dealing with that day.
In response to an earlier round of discovery disputes, the court said that the BBC was entitled to information shedding light on the “message” of the speech and the “impression” it left. But the court said also said then it was not giving the media company a green light to “relitigate” the events of January 6.
In total, the BBC has issued at least 47 subpoenas to former and current government officials, as well as private advisers in Trump’s circle, who had a window into his efforts to overturn the election – including Jared Kushner and Ivanka Trump, former Attorney General Bill Barr, and former White House counsel Pat Cipollone.
The judge punted on a dispute over whether former special counsel Jack Smith can be deposed by the defendants. She is requiring that Smith and BBC go through the formal process of seeking the approval from his former employer, the Justice Department, for his deposition, and the judge said they could return to the question once DOJ responds.
Why BBC wants to depose Trump
Ordering a December 11 deadline for the deposition, Lett noted that she did not have the power to move back the current December 18 end date for discovery in the case. Trump could ask the US district court judge overseeing the lawsuit to extend that discovery deadline, she said, opening up the possibility for a delay of the deposition.
Lett will rule in writing over a series of objections Trump’s team has issued to documents sought by BBC or questions that they want him to answer. Some of those demands have to do with the January 6 speech, while other requests deal with information about his businesses, and even polling data about his favorability.
In seeking the Mar-a-Lago records, BBC wants to test Trump’s claims that the documentary harmed his profession – and specifically his “profession, occupation and trade”– Tobin said Thursday, quoting from the current version of the complaint. The BBC is seeking records indicating its membership numbers and the dues for those memberships over a six-year span since before the documentary aired.
Trump’s original lawsuit sought damages related to the alleged harm to his businesses and brand, but in August amended it to narrow that alleged harm to his personal reputation.
Lett ultimately agreed with the BBC that removing claims of damages to Trump’s business did not shut the door to probing Mar-a-Lago’s popularity as a metric for alleged harm to Trump’s professional reputation, given the role the resort has played in his presidency.
This story has been updated with additional developments.

Judge in Miami says Trump must sit for deposition in BBC defamation lawsuit by Dec. 11
Washington — A federal judge said President Trump must sit for a deposition with lawyers for the BBC by Dec. 11 as part of his ongoing defamation lawsuit against the British broadcaster.
U.S. Magistrate Judge Enjolique Lett set the deadline during a hearing in Miami on Thursday morning, according to the Associated Press. The judge ordered Mr. Trump to answer questions by Dec. 11 or face penalties, which could include dismissal of his lawsuit against the BBC, unless the period for the president and the network to collect information in the case is extended, the AP reported.
Mr. Trump was supposed to sit for a deposition Friday, but his lawyers told the BBC late last month that he would no longer be available to answer questions "due to other matters of national importance." The BBC told the court that on the day of the scheduled deposition, Oct. 16, the president spoke at a rally in Georgia alongside GOP candidates for the Senate and governor. He then traveled to his South Florida resort, Mar-a-Lago, where he attended an event for the Republican National Committee.
The president said he would be available for the deposition in the second or third week of January, according to the BBC.
Lawyers for the broadcaster had asked the judge to compel Mr. Trump to confirm a date for the deposition and answer their questions.
In a statement, a spokesman for the president's legal team did not address the judge's demand for a deposition, but said his "powerhouse lawsuit is holding the BBC accountable for its defamation and reckless election interference just as he has held other fake news mainstream media responsible for their wrongdoing."
Mr. Trump filed his $10 billion lawsuit against the BBC in December over a documentary that featured spliced-together portions of a speech he gave outside the White House on Jan. 6, 2021. Mr. Trump alleged that the documentary, which aired in October 2024, just weeks before the presidential election, misled viewers and falsely depicted his remarks to supporters.
Following the president's speech, a crowd of his backers marched to the U.S. Capitol and breached the building, where lawmakers and then-Vice President Mike Pence were gathered to reaffirm the results of the 2020 election.
The BBC said in November 2025 that it "sincerely regrets" how the clip of Mr. Trump's speech was edited but disagreed that there was a basis for a defamation claim. The network apologized to the president.
At the hearing Thursday, lawyers for the BBC and the president were set to discuss the network's subpoena for deposition testimony from Jack Smith, the former special counsel who brought criminal charges against Mr. Trump in 2023. The case involved Mr. Trump's alleged efforts to subvert the transfer of presidential power after the 2020 election. The charges were dismissed after the president was elected to a second term in 2024.
In defending the subpoena for Smith's testimony, the BBC said in a court filing that the former special counsel could shed light on matters involving Mr. Trump's speech on Jan. 6, including whether the president knew his remarks could lead to violence. The network said Smith does not object to the subpoena.
But Mr. Trump's lawyers refuted the notion that Smith has personal knowledge about the president's speech or state of mind when he delivered it. They also said Smith's testimony would be "duplicative," since he authored a final report on his investigation and testified twice to Congress about his case against Mr. Trump.
The BBC is also seeking documents from Mar-a-Lago about its membership and initiation fees, which the president's lawyers argue does not serve a legitimate purpose.
The discovery process began in February and is set to end Dec. 18. BBC lawyers said in a filing that nearly eight months into discovery, they still have not spoken with Mr. Trump and do not have a schedule to question him. They called the president "the most central figure in this case."
"There is hardly a more crucial and relevant piece of discovery in a defamation lawsuit than the deposition of the Plaintiff. For that reason, a plaintiff's unwillingness to sit for a deposition can be perilous to his claim," they wrote in a motion earlier this month.

sources.text:
Donald Trump must submit to questioning in his $10 billion defamation lawsuit against the BBC by December 11, a federal judge has ruled. Failure to appear could put the case at risk of dismissal.
US Magistrate Judge Enjoliqué Lett set the deadline during a hearing in Miami on Thursday after BBC attorneys accused Trump of repeatedly delaying his deposition.
“With two months left in the discovery period, we still haven’t been able to depose the plaintiff,” BBC lawyer Charles Tobin told the court.
The parties had agreed that Trump would be questioned on October 16. He later canceled the meeting, citing a “matter of national importance.”
Tobin said Trump was instead in Georgia campaigning.
“He was participating in party politics and prioritized that over sitting for the deposition,” Tobin said.
Judge Lett warned that Trump could face sanctions—including dismissal of the lawsuit—if he misses the new deadline, unless the discovery schedule is extended beyond December 18.
Trump filed the Florida lawsuit last December over a BBC Panorama documentary that edited together portions of his January 6, 2021, speech in a way he says falsely suggested he called for violence at the US Capitol.
Trump speaks at a campaign rally in Pendleton, South Carolina, on Wednesday
The BBC apologized for the editing but has denied defaming Trump. The controversy led to the resignations of director-general Tim Davie and news chief Deborah Turness.
The broadcaster has asked the court to dismiss the case, arguing that the documentary was not broadcast in Florida or elsewhere in the United States. It also maintains that Trump’s allegations fall “well short of the high bar of actual malice” required for a public figure to prevail.
BBC lawyers further argued that Trump “cannot plausibly claim that the documentary harmed his reputation,” noting that he won the 2024 election a week after the program aired and carried Florida by a wide margin.
“Indeed, the documentary was prescient in accurately describing the loyalty plaintiff enjoys among his supporters, and that led to his return to the White House,” the BBC said in its motion.
In a court filing dated October 13, BBC lawyers said they began requesting possible deposition dates in July and followed up repeatedly before the two sides settled on October 16.
According to the filing, the broadcaster heard nothing for several weeks. Then, on September 28, Trump’s attorney said, “the President is no longer available for his deposition on October 16 due to other matters of national importance.”
The attorney pledged to “endeavor to provide you with a replacement date by the end of this week,” the filing said. “He did not,” BBC lawyers wrote.
Trump’s legal team subsequently told the BBC that he “has no availability whatsoever for a deposition” before discovery ends on December 18. They offered instead to make him available during the second or third week of January.
“Two months of discovery remaining, the BBC still has not been able to depose, and does not even have a schedule to depose, the most central figure in this case: Plaintiff himself,” Tobin wrote.
The BBC is also seeking testimony from Ivanka Trump, Jared Kushner and Donald Trump Jr. The broadcaster told the court that Trump’s two eldest children were present when he revised his January 6 speech and when he delivered it.
The BBC says Kushner prepared a statement condemning the Capitol attack that was never released by the White House. Trump’s attorneys have accused the broadcaster of pursuing “politically-driven leverage” against the president by targeting his family.

Trump speaks to his supporters outside the White House on January 6, 2021
Police turned away the BBC’s process servers at Ivanka and Kushner’s Miami home in May, and a Secret Service lawyer later said the agency was not authorized to accept subpoenas for them. A bid to serve Don Jr at Trump Tower also failed.
Lett cleared the way on October 9, allowing the BBC to serve the trio by certified mail to their home and business addresses and by email to Trump’s lawyers. The ruling does not settle any objections to the scope of the subpoenas.
Lawyers for both sides tussled on Thursday over the BBC’s separate bid to depose Jack Smith, the former special counsel who brought the federal January 6 case against Trump. The president strongly opposes the move.
Smith charged Trump in August 2023 with four felony counts over his bid to overturn the 2020 election, but the case was dropped after his 2024 victory under a Justice Department policy barring the prosecution of a sitting president.
The broadcaster subpoenaed Smith earlier this month, but Trump’s lawyers argued in a joint filing that there was no reason for Smith, who is not a party to the case, to appear.
‘Smith lacks any personal knowledge regarding the issues in this matter,’ they wrote. ‘He was not present when President Trump’s January 6, 2021, speech… was made, nor did he participate in its preparation.’
Trump’s team also argued that ‘Smith’s testimony would be duplicative,’ pointing out that he published a lengthy report on January 6 and testified for hours. ‘The entirety of his testimony is publicly available,’ the filing said.
‘It is difficult to imagine a more authoritative source on these issues than Mr. Smith, who spent years gathering evidence on those topics with the force of the Justice Department and the power of the grand jury behind him,’ the BBC’s lawyers countered.
‘No one forced Plaintiff to file this lawsuit and to dispute that his speech on January 6 incited the violence that followed at the Capitol,’ they added.
Smith never charged Trump with incitement and wrote in his final report released in January 2025 that prosecutors did not develop direct evidence of ‘Trump’s subjective intent to cause the full scope of the violence that occurred on Jan. 6.’

As the president’s dwindling popularity keeps setting records, more and more people are showing up to his pre-midterm election rallies to heckle and protest him. Texas Governor Greg Abbott is pretending sheriffs endorsed him when they never did.
Texas Governor Greg Abbott
Sergio Flores/Getty Images
Texas Governor Greg Abbott
Texas Republican Governor Greg Abbott publicized the endorsements of 11 Democratic sheriffs. Three of them denied ever endorsing him.
Zapata County Sheriff Ramon Montes, Val Verde County Sheriff Joe Frank Martinez, and Webb County Sheriff Marin Cuellar all publicly announced that they were not endorsing Abbot after he posted them on his endorsement list on Monday. While Cuellar has been removed from the list, Montes and Martinez are still on it.
“Please remove my name from this for the Governor Abbott. This is Sheriff Martin Cuellar. The governor endorsed Tano my brother’s opponent,” Cuellar wrote in a text screenshot he posted on Facebook. Cuellar is the brother of Democratic Representative Henry Cuellar, who is currently running for Texas’s 28th House district.
“I want to make it unequivocally clear that I have not issued a political endorsement of Governor Greg Abbott, and I did not authorize anyone to use my name as an endorsement,” Martinez wrote in his own official statement. “I made it clear to the Sheriff who submitted the endorsement that I could not endorse Governor Abbott. Sheriff Montes’s office told Border Report that he “is not endorsing anyone at this time.”

MIAMI (CN) — President Donald Trump must sit for a deposition in his $10 billion defamation lawsuit against the British Broadcasting Corporation, a federal judge ruled Thursday.
U.S. Magistrate Judge Enjoliqué Lett set a deadline of Dec. 11, warning another delay could result in dismissal of the case.
Trump filed the defamation lawsuit in Miami federal court last year over a documentary aired by the BBC that included an edited portion of a speech he gave before the U.S. Capitol riot on Jan. 6, 2021, that appeared to show the president directing supporters to attack.
Trump claimed the documentary, which aired a week before the 2024 presidential election, attempted to “interfere in and influence the election’s outcome to President Trump’s detriment.”
BBC chairman Samir Shah sent an apology to Trump shortly after the documentary’s release, calling the clip an “error of judgment.” Trump nevertheless sued the news outlet, seeking $10 billion in damages.
Trump has repeatedly avoided his deposition since July, citing “matters of national importance.” The parties finally agreed on Oct. 16, but Trump cancelled a week prior, claiming no availability this year.
The latest cancellation prompted the BBC to ask the judge to compel the president to comply in a motion filed last week.
“Nearly eight months into discovery, after seven depositions of BBC witnesses, and with only two months of discovery remaining, the BBC still has not been able to depose, and does not even have a schedule to depose, the most central figure in this case,” the BBC said in its motion. “There is hardly a more crucial and relevant piece of discovery in a defamation lawsuit than the deposition of the plaintiff. For that reason, a plaintiff’s unwillingness to sit for a deposition can be perilous to his claim.”
The BBC also pushed back against Trump’s claims that national security matters prevented his deposition, he attended campaign events on Oct. 16, including a fundraiser at his Mar-a-Lago home in Florida.
In response, Trump accused the BBC of a “pattern of improperly, prematurely, and unilaterally filing motions for discovery hearing” and not “taking into account the singular nature of his role in our system of government, the complexity of his schedule and the national security implications involved.”
“Those matters include, but are not limited to, the conflict in Iran, unrest in other parts of the Middle East, the war between Russia and Ukraine, the White House accord on super intelligence and other matters that have significantly impacted the United States’ national security and economy,” he said.
Trump also asked the court to bar video recording of the deposition, an unusual request rejected by Lett during Thursday’s hearing.
In a statement, a spokesman for Trump’s legal team did not directly address the judge’s decision.
“The BBC has a long pattern of deceiving its audience in coverage of President Trump, all in service of its own leftist political agenda,” the spokesman said. “President Trump’s powerhouse lawsuit is holding the BBC accountable for its defamation and reckless election interference just as he has held other fake news mainstream media responsible for their wrongdoing.”

sources.news_title: Trump BBC Lawsuit: Testify by Dec. 11 or Face Dismissal
sources.text:
Donald Trump has been ordered to testify under oath by December 11 in the $10 billion defamation lawsuit he filed against the BBC, with a federal judge warning that failure to cooperate could cost him the entire case.
The latest development in the Trump BBC lawsuit came Thursday, October 22, when U.S. Magistrate Judge Enjoliqué Lett set a firm deadline following complaints that Trump had repeatedly delayed his deposition. According to the Associated Press, attorneys representing the British broadcaster told the Miami court they had been unable to question Trump despite months of attempts to arrange his testimony.
BBC attorney Charles Tobin expressed frustration with the delays, telling the judge that “we still haven’t been able to depose the plaintiff.”
The dispute centers on a deposition originally scheduled for October 16. Attorneys for Trump canceled that appearance, citing a “matter of national importance.” However, Tobin argued that Trump spent the day campaigning in Georgia rather than attending to an urgent government obligation.
“He was participating in party politics and prioritized that over sitting for the deposition,” Tobin said.
Judge Lett responded by ordering Trump to complete his deposition no later than December 11. According to the Associated Press, she warned that continued noncompliance could result in sanctions, including dismissal of the lawsuit, unless the court extends the existing discovery schedule.
The discovery deadline currently falls on December 18, leaving attorneys just one week between Trump’s required testimony and the scheduled conclusion of evidence gathering.
During discovery, opposing attorneys can request documents, question witnesses under oath, and obtain information relevant to their claims and defenses. Because Trump personally initiated the lawsuit, BBC attorneys argue that questioning him is essential to understanding the allegations he wants the court to consider.
The judge explained that changes to the broader case schedule must be approved by the presiding judge. BBC attorneys indicated they would consider a later deposition if the discovery and trial schedules were officially extended.
The Trump BBC lawsuit dates back to December 2025, when Trump sued the publicly funded broadcaster over its documentary, “Trump: A Second Chance.” He accused the organization of defamation and deceptive and unfair trade practices, seeking $10 billion in damages.
The documentary controversy involves footage from Trump’s January 6, 2021, speech in Washington, delivered before his supporters stormed the U.S. Capitol.
According to BBC reporting, producers combined statements from separate portions of Trump’s speech, delivered nearly an hour apart, creating the impression that he had directly encouraged supporters to engage in violent action.
The broadcaster subsequently acknowledged that the editing created a misleading impression and apologized. The controversy also preceded the resignations of BBC director general Tim Davie and news chief Deborah Turness.
Despite acknowledging the editing mistake, the BBC has rejected Trump’s allegations that the documentary legally defamed him. The broadcaster has also challenged the lawsuit on jurisdictional grounds, arguing that the disputed program was not broadcast or made available through its platforms in the United States.
Those competing positions remain central to the Trump BBC lawsuit, which now involves disagreements over what evidence the broadcaster should be permitted to collect.
According to The Guardian’s reporting from Thursday’s hearing, Judge Lett also rejected an effort by Trump’s legal team to prevent his deposition from being recorded on video. The questioning is expected to last seven hours, although access to the recording will be restricted to attorneys involved in the case.
The judge additionally raised concerns about the documents produced by Trump’s legal team. The Guardian reported that she gave his attorneys 30 days to provide relevant materials after questioning whether they had conducted a sufficient search for responsive records.
Another major disagreement involves former special counsel Jack Smith, whom the BBC subpoenaed earlier in October as part of its defense.
Smith previously investigated Trump’s actions surrounding January 6, and BBC attorneys believe his findings and knowledge could help address disputed issues in the lawsuit.
Trump’s lawyers disagree and have challenged the effort to obtain Smith’s testimony.
“Smith lacks any personal knowledge regarding the issues in this matter,” Trump’s attorneys argued in a joint court filing. “He was not present when President Trump’s January 6, 2021, speech … was made, nor did he participate in its preparation. Smith does not have any personal knowledge regarding President Trump’s state of mind at the time the Speech was given.”
The legal team further contended that “Smith’s testimony would be duplicative,” pointing to his previous investigative report and extensive testimony about January 6.
“The entirety of his testimony is publicly available,” Trump’s attorneys argued.
BBC lawyers rejected that reasoning, emphasizing the depth of Smith’s investigation and the evidence his team collected while examining events surrounding the Capitol attack.
“It is difficult to imagine a more authoritative source on these issues than Mr. Smith, who spent years gathering evidence on those topics with the force of the Justice Department and the power of the grand jury behind him,” the BBC’s lawyers argued.
The broadcaster also maintains that Trump cannot pursue substantial financial damages while preventing its attorneys from accessing evidence necessary to defend against his accusations.
“No one forced Plaintiff to file this lawsuit and to dispute that his speech on January 6 incited the violence that followed at the Capitol. But as long as he chooses to maintain the case, he cannot commit the fundamental injustice of preventing the BBC from obtaining the evidence it needs to robustly defend itself on every element of his claim.”
The filing has also faced procedural challenges beyond the deposition fight. According to the BBC, Trump dropped claims against two BBC Studios companies in July while continuing his lawsuit against the British Broadcasting Corporation itself.
Although the broadcaster has apologized for the documentary edit, neither that apology nor the executive resignations establish legal liability for defamation. The underlying claims remain contested.
